content: Community-based HIV testing services (HTS) involve offering HIV testing outside of traditional healthcare facilities, directly within community settings. This approach was recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2013 to increase testing coverage, particularly among key populations such as young people, men, and individuals less likely to access facility-based testing. Community-based HTS can be implemented in various ways, including fixed community sites, mobile outreach in hotspots, and at locations like parks, bars, clubs, saunas, workplaces, educational institutions, and places of worship. Mobile vans are often used to facilitate these services. Testing can also be conducted at individuals' homes, referred to as home-based HTS, which may involve door-to-door testing or targeted testing, such as for HIV partner services. Community-based HTS is often delivered by trained lay providers or peers using rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) and triage testing strategies. These services can be offered alone or integrated with testing for other infections like tuberculosis (TB), viral hepatitis, and sexually transmitted infections (STIs), or as part of broader community health services, such as maternal and child health or family planning. Proper training and supervision of providers are essential when combining HTS with other services. WHO recommends community-based HTS in high HIV burden settings, linking individuals to prevention, treatment, and care services. This recommendation applies to all populations, with a particular focus on key populations. In low HIV burden settings, community-based HTS is recommended specifically for key populations, again with linkage to appropriate services. These recommendations are based on strong evidence, though the quality of evidence is considered low. As of July 2019, 82% of reporting countries globally were using community-based HTS approaches. A systematic review identified nearly 500 studies on community-based HTS outcomes, with most published between 2015 and 2018. These studies demonstrated high uptake of community-based HTS among both general and key populations, with pooled uptake rates of 82% and 80%, respectively. The review also highlighted differences in uptake based on the community-based HTS model and target population. For example, workplace HTS reached the highest proportion of men (91%), and nearly half of those tested in the general population were first-time testers, compared to over two-thirds among key populations. The review found that community-based HTS achieved high rates of new HIV diagnoses, with 76% of diagnoses in the general population and 89% in key populations being new. Linkage to treatment or care varied by local epidemiology, setting, and population but was generally comparable to facility-based HTS. Pooled linkage estimates were 62% for the general population and 81% for key populations. However, linkage rates may be underestimated due to loss to follow-up or individuals already on antiretroviral therapy (ART). Combining community-based HTS with testing for other infections, such as STIs and TB, was shown to be feasible and effective, achieving high HIV testing uptake. For example, pooled HTS uptake was 95% when combined with STI testing and 91–93% when combined with both STI and TB testing. However, uptake was lower when HTS was combined only with TB testing (71%) or other chronic conditions (67–77%). Community-based HTS has become a key component of national HTS plans in many countries. When implementing community-based HTS, several factors should be considered: 1. Timing and Frequency: Services can be offered continuously, on a regular schedule, or as one-time events. Continuous services may be more appropriate for men and young people in high HIV burden settings or key populations with low HTS uptake. Outreach at convenient times, such as evenings or weekends, is important for priority populations. 2. Focused Services: Community-based HTS should target populations and settings with the greatest unmet testing needs. Evidence shows that focused services can effectively reach first-time testers and individuals with undiagnosed HIV infections. 3. Resource Use: The cost and cost-effectiveness of community-based HTS vary widely depending on local epidemiology, populations reached, and delivery costs. Focused approaches that identify more people with HIV are likely to be more cost-effective. 4. Linkage to Services: Ensuring linkage to prevention, treatment, and care services is critical. Additional support may be needed for certain populations, such as transgender individuals, people who inject drugs, and those diagnosed through home-based HTS. Effective referral pathways to prevention services are also essential for individuals testing HIV-negative but at ongoing risk. 5. Workplace HTS: This approach is effective for reaching men in high burden settings, such as mining operations, transport sectors, and informal work environments. Workplace HTS should be implemented within policies that ensure confidentiality and protect workers from discrimination. 6. Mobile Outreach: Mobile HTS can complement facility-based services in areas with low coverage and poor accessibility, particularly for key populations and men. 7. Faith-based HTS: Faith-based settings offer a promising avenue for HTS, and the use of HIV self-testing (HIVST) kits in these settings can improve acceptability. 8. Home-based HTS: This approach can reach undiagnosed individuals in high burden settings, particularly men, if offered outside of work hours. Home-based combination prevention interventions, including HTS, have been shown to reduce HIV incidence when high coverage is achieved. 9. Community Campaigns: These campaigns can serve rural and remote populations with limited access to facility-based HTS. However, they may not be effective in low burden settings unless focused on priority populations. 10. School-based HTS: While not optimal for reaching undiagnosed HIV infections, school-based programs in high burden settings can provide opportunities for broader HIV prevention and sexual health education, particularly for adolescent girls. 11. Combination Services: Integrating HTS with testing and screening for other infections and conditions is feasible and effective, especially for key populations. This strategy can optimize resource use and improve efficiency. HIV self-testing (HIVST) allows individuals to collect their own specimens (oral fluid or blood), perform the test, and interpret the results at their convenience. WHO strongly recommends HIVST as an additional HTS approach, particularly for individuals at ongoing risk who need frequent testing. HIVST has proven effective in expanding HTS among populations less likely to test otherwise. Various service delivery models for HIVST include online or phone-based kit requests, facility-based distribution, home or community-based distribution, and secondary distribution by clients to their peers or partners.
